title: Virginia-based nonprofit on the ground in Nepal - 12onyourside.com
description: Virginia-based nonprofit on the ground in Nepal  12onyourside.com
publisher.title: 12onyourside.com
full_article:
RICHMOND, Va. (WWBT) - A Virginia-based nonprofit is on the ground in Nepal delivering food to families impacted by the catastrophic flood.

Mercy Chefs often provides hot meals to those in need, but pivoted to grocery packs for Nepal’s unique situation.

Many places are only accessible by helicopter.

“Most of the bridges have been wiped out. So, to get to the communities on the far side, you have to go hours around to find a bridge that’s operable to get to that community, and these people didn’t have margin beforehand. What little they had is now either gone or it’s under 20 or 30 feet of mud at this point,” Mercy Chefs Chief Global Officer Carl Ladd said.

Ladd was on the ground in Nuwakot on Tuesday, September 1, and has been in the country for several days now. In that time, he and his team have helped provide around 75,000 meals.

The packs contain 30 days of food rations, so people will be set for the coming days.

“Most of the families we’re distributing to have lost loved ones; they’ve lost their home, they’ve lost their livelihood, they’ve lost their farm. So it’s devastating,” Ladd said.

Mercy Chefs is working with local Nepali organizations throughout the effort, which Ladd says has been key.

Ladd has been on the ground for other natural disasters, and says typically in floods there’s a couple feet of sediment, but this time the debris extends all throughout the river valley.

“In most of these places there’s still 20 feet of sediment and so two-story buildings are underneath mud for whole towns,” Ladd said.

Ladd describes the entire experience as humbling, from seeing a sigh of relief on a mother’s face, to working with local volunteers.

Virginians are among some of the people still unaccounted for, which puts things in perspective for the Mercy Chefs team. Its crew is keeping them and their loved ones in mind during the mission.

“I would say that’s a really unique thing about this disaster is the amount of foreigners that were affected. Obviously, it’s a really popular destination and valley for trekking,” Ladd said. “It makes the world a little bit smaller and it hit a little bit more closer to home. And realizing that the international community is affected and obviously the Nepalese communities is largely affected.”

Mercy Chefs will continue to be in Nepal as long as its team is needed. Donations to the effort can be made here.

title: S.C. nonprofit deploys clean water teams to Nepal disaster zone - WRDW
description: S.C. nonprofit deploys clean water teams to Nepal disaster zone  WRDW
publisher.title: WRDW
full_article:
CHARLESTON, S.C. (WRDW/WAGT) - Water Mission disaster response teams, including people from the Charleston area, arrived in the Nepal-China border region Tuesday, with some already traveling to deliver aid, following mudslides and flash floods that struck nearly a week ago.

Mount Pleasant resident Kristin Parker said she is concerned for loved ones in the area.

Her family lived in Nepal for 13 years, and she has visited the border region where the flooding originated, keeping close ties with villagers there.

“It’s horrible for me to think about when I watch it from a different distance, but to really know people that are living it,” Kristin Parker, cofounder of Shared City and Mount Pleasant resident, said.

As of today, CBS reports at least 1,050 dead and over 4,600 missing in Nepal.

Across the border in Tibet, Chinese officials confirm 16 deaths and more than 550 people still missing.

Officials in Nepal say a massive rock and ice avalanche in the mountains likely triggered the flooding.

According to CBS News, 85 Americans are still listed as missing.

“We’re still finding out the extent of the loss, but even already we know that there are some families where there’s only one family member left,” Parker said.

Search teams have rescued more than 11,000 survivors, but many remain cut off from basic necessities.

Charleston-based Water Mission is deploying teams with specialized testing gear to secure safe water.

“Water supply is often contaminated or non-existent and in order to rebuild and restart, having access to safe drinking water is so important,” said Gregg Dinino, public relations director for Water Mission.

On-the-ground engineers are testing local sources, installing treatment systems and teaching local volunteers how to keep them running.

“It’s difficult; they’re very hard to reach areas, you have to traverse a mountain into the Himalayas. Many of these roads have been knocked out. We’ve heard from contacts on the ground that what used to take 45 minutes to get to an area now takes six to seven hours,” Dinino said.

The organization sets up tap stands to serve as central distribution points for residents.

By treating water directly at the source, the systems can generate thousands of gallons daily, enough to supply up to 5,000 survivors each day.

“So thankful for the work they do and I just feel so relieved that they’re going to be on the ground to care about the people that I love so much there,” Parker said.

Dinino said local volunteers in Charleston are critical for assembling and preparing equipment for disaster relief.

He said the duration of their deployment relies heavily on donations.

Those interested in volunteering or donating through Water Mission can find more information on the Water Mission website.

आइ धरि सीबीएस नेपाल मे कम सँ कम १०५० गोटेक मृत्यु आ ४६०० सँ बेसी लापता होयबाक सूचना अछि ।

नेपाल के अधिकारी के कहनाय छनि जे पहाड़ मे भारी चट्टान आओर बर्फ के हिमस्खलन सं संभवतः बाढ़ि के शुरुआत भेल छल.

सीबीएस न्यूज के अनुसार 85 अमेरिकी एखनो लापता के रूप मे सूचीबद्ध अछि.

पार्कर कहलनि जे, हम सब एखनो नुकसान के हद के पता लगा रहल छी, मुदा पहिने सं सेहो हमरा सब के पता अछि जे किछु एहन परिवार अछि जतय परिवार के एकटा सदस्य मात्र बचि गेल अछि.

खोज टीम 11 हजार स बेसी बचि गेल लोक कए बचा लेलक अछि, मुदा बहुतो लोक बुनियादी जरूरत स कटल अछि।

चार्ल्सटन स्थित वाटर मिशन सुरक्षित पानी क॑ सुरक्षित रखै लेली विशेष परीक्षण गियर वाला टीम क॑ तैनात करी रहलऽ छै ।

जल मिशन केरऽ जनसंपर्क निदेशक ग्रेग डिनिनो न॑ कहलकै कि पानी केरऽ आपूर्ति अक्सर दूषित या गैर-मौजूद होय छै आरू एकरऽ पुनर्निर्माण आरू पुनः आरंभ करै लेली सुरक्षित पेयजल केरऽ पहुँच एतना जरूरी छै ।

जमीन पर इंजीनियर स्थानीय स्रोत कें परीक्षण कयर रहल छै, उपचार प्रणाली लगा रहल छै आ स्थानीय स्वयंसेवक कें सिखा रहल छै कि ओकरा कोना चलाएल जै.

सीधा स्रोत पर पानी कें उपचार सं इ सिस्टम रोजाना हजारक गैलन कें उत्पादन कयर सकय छै, जे हर दिन 5,000 बचे वाला लोगक कें आपूर्ति कें लेल पर्याप्त छै.

ROBBINSVILLE, N.J. (WPVI) -- As rescue efforts continue following the deadly flash flooding in Nepal, a New Jersey woman is among those reported missing, while relief organizations work to assist survivors.

BAPS Swaminarayan Akshardham in Robbinsville, the largest Hindu temple in the United States, is among the organizations helping support relief efforts.

The temple, which volunteers say has welcomed more than 4 million visitors over the past three years, is known as a place where many come to find peace.

READ MORE | Death toll tops 1,000 after Nepal flooding, as search continues for thousands

Rescuers are desperately searching for survivors after the devastating flooding on the border of Nepal and Tibet.

"The fundamental idea is to be a good person," said volunteer Yogesh Patel.

That message has taken on added significance as members of the temple and the larger BAPS temple community respond to flash floods in Nepal that have killed more than 1,000 people.

Patel said the scale and speed of the disaster were difficult to comprehend.

"It just seemed like this is not possible how can a wall of water that big literally go down a hill into valley and flood areas in seconds?" Patel said.

The Robbinsville temple is one of several BAPS temples sending aid to Nepal through a group in India. Patel said BAPS volunteers in Nepal began relief efforts immediately after the disaster.

"We actually have a center in Nepal, so our volunteers with BAPS from day 1 were active in trying to get grains, rice, lentils, food, cooking utensils and getting it to the worst affected areas as soon as possible," Patel said.

In addition to providing supplies, the temple's spiritual leader has offered prayers for those who died and for the thousands of people who remain unaccounted for. Those reported missing include Mukti Belahal of Princeton Junction.

"For those loved ones to not know where their loved ones are, it really is crushing," Patel said.

As search-and-rescue operations continue, volunteers say efforts to deliver food, supplies and other necessities to affected communities remain ongoing.

"Our hearts immediately go out to those who are suffering in this," Patel said.

Temple leaders said they hope the spirit of service promoted at BAPS Swaminarayan Akshardham encourages others to offer positive thoughts and prayers for those affected by the disaster in Nepal.

title: Live updates: Warning signs were visible ahead of Nepal-China floods, report says - CNN
description: Live updates: Warning signs were visible ahead of Nepal-China floods, report says  CNNDeath toll from devastating floods in Nepal and China surpasses 1,000  Al JazeeraScenes of devastation in Nuwakot district after Nepal flash floods kill hundreds of people  Yahoo
publisher.title: CNN
full_article:
The glacier that collapsed causing a devastating landslide and flooding had visible signs of change days ahead of the disaster, according to a new report from a consortium of scientists.

“In hindsight, there were some pre-event indications,” including melt water that had turned visibly brown and signs of a crack propagating into the surrounding bedrock slope days before the collapse, scientists said in a report published last week.

The report – which also suggests more comprehensive early warning systems downstream could have saved a “significant number of lives” – comes as the catastrophe has shown what experts say is a need for better warning systems in a vast Himalayan region that is difficult to monitor.

Chinese and Nepali authorities had met as recently as May to discuss bolstering cooperation on monitoring natural hazards in the Himalayas, a government official who was present at that meeting told CNN.

Early warning systems had been set up recently in this region, focusing on several glacial lakes in China, but no operational system was set up in this area for glacier-related hazards, according to the report from the HiRISK scientific consortium, which monitors risk data in mountain environments.

Once the collapse started, however, the warning times from conventional systems would have likely been insufficient for evacuation at a border checkpoint that was among the first areas hit – given just how fast the initial landslide was moving. Further downstream, with warning times of 10 minutes or more, comprehensive systems could have saved lives, the scientists said.

Other experts have said that the glacial collapse highlights the urgency of better monitoring programs – and cooperation between countries – to detect changes.

“There is almost no way that anyone could have detected this event prior – it happened in a blind spot … (making it) extremely difficult to detect,” Austin Lord, a senior fellow in the Energy, Water and Sustainability program at the Stimson Center, wrote in a recent commentary.

He also highlighted “how greater communication, information sharing, and collaborative analysis of transboundary risks between Nepal and China are sorely needed.”

KATHMANDU, Nepal (AP) — Rescue teams with search dogs continued to search through mud, rocks and debris on Tuesday on the border with Nepal and China for thousands of people still missing following the catastrophic floods that tore through communities across the Himalayas , leaving more than 1,000 dead.

As police in Kathmandu buried dozens of bodies in multiple trenches, Nepal’s disaster agency said that 1,003 deaths had been counted there, with 3,916 people missing, including 583 foreign nationals. In its latest update, China reported 16 deaths and 546 missing, including 261 foreigners.

The scale of the Aug. 26 disaster is hampering rescue efforts in both countries, with landslides, destroyed roads and widespread damage cutting off remote areas. Crews faced challenging conditions as they searched unstable terrain and piles of debris, raising fears the death toll could rise as rescuers reach isolated communities.

At least 168 people were killed and more than 1,300 were missing after catastrophic and deadly torrents of floods and mud swept through several communities along the Nepal-China following a glacier collapse.

Mass burials of unidentified bodies in Kathmandu

In Kathmandu, police worked in heavy rain on Tuesday to bury dozens of bodies in multiple trenches next to a forested area.

Barbed wire was erected around the site, while blue numbered markers identified the graves of people whose names were not yet known.

Authorities in Nepal have been burying bodies in temporary graves until they can be identified. They are preserving DNA samples, photographing distinguishing facial features and recording other identifying details.

Each body is assigned a reference number to help families identify and claim the remains later.

Relief operations expanded to stranded communities

At least 11,814 people have been rescued so far, according to Nepalese authorities. Emergency crews used helicopters and other aircraft to reach stranded communities in areas where roads and bridges have been destroyed by the flooding and landslides.

Efforts are being stepped up to provide assistance to survivors in areas where roads and other transportation routes had been damaged or cut off.

China’s Foreign Ministry spokesperson, Guo Jiakun, said a second batch of relief supplies was being sent to Nepal, including drones, DNA testing and water purification equipment. Chinese DNA testing experts will also help Nepal identify bodies, he said.

Bimal Sharma, a helicopter pilot who has been flying rescue and relief missions, said he was shocked to see the devastation in Timure, a border town close to Tibet that he has known for years.

“It felt like I was flying over an entirely different landscape,” said Sharma, adding that he has had little opportunity to speak with the people he rescued. “I can see the pain in their eyes. It’s heartbreaking,” he said.

The disaster began in the Himalayas when a glacial collapse sent large amounts of rock, ice and meltwater into valleys below, triggering powerful floods downstream.

Scientists studying satellite imagery said the collapse appears to have involved the failure of bedrock beneath a glacier in the Himalayan region. The rockfall was powerful enough to register as a magnitude 5.2 seismic event.

The resulting surge of water and debris entered rivers that flow through valleys in Tibet and Nepal, causing them to rise rapidly. Floodwaters swept away homes, buildings, roads and bridges and carried mud and rocks downstream.

title: Prakrit has already lost her father. As Nepal’s morgues fill, she hopes her DNA can be used to find her mother - theguardian.com
description: Prakrit has already lost her father. As Nepal’s morgues fill, she hopes her DNA can be used to find her mother  theguardian.com
publisher.title: theguardian.com
full_article:
An army official calls out a name. A young woman stands, two pieces of identification in her hands. She fills out a form, takes another and moves to the back of the hospital to give a vial of blood.

With so many people killed by Nepal’s floods, and hundreds of bodies being buried because the morgues are full, there is now a push to identify victims through DNA. The woman, Prakrit Gurung, 19, is hoping her DNA will be linked to her mother’s body. Her father’s has been found – her brother recognised his picture on a wall outside the hospital.

View image in fullscreen Prakrit Gurung (second from left) outside the hospital. Photograph: Sonam Choekyi/The Guardian

At the government’s request, Gurung is one of dozens lining up on Tuesday morning. Earlier, an Australian citizen was one of the first 14 people to attend. He had flown over to be with his family – his brother, a Nepali citizen, is missing.

Authorities are asking relatives abroad to have their DNA profiles sent over. Several Australian families have already had samples taken.

“We are collecting the blood samples here, from their siblings, or direct relatives,” says Rameshwor Adhikari from the army. “People are coming from all over the valley to give blood, and from different places all over the country.”

DNA testing offers hope to families searching for Nepal flood victims – video

Adhikari adds: “It is a disaster. A natural calamity.”

The first day they set up 37 people came through but numbers are growing – and the army brings out more shade tents for people to sit under.

Adhikari wants as many people as possible to come forward. There are now more than 1,000 people confirmed dead and nearly 4,000 reported missing. As of Wednesday morning, 38 of them are Australians.

View image in fullscreen Hospital workers prepare to take blood samples. Photograph: Sonam Choekyi/The Guardian

In a statement this week, family members of 25 missing Australians called for more government support to “bring our friends and loved ones back home”.

Nepali families from the worst-hit area, the upper Rasuwa district, have been campaigning for their government to do more to get boots and rescue equipment on the ground.

It has been a week since the floods and contact has still not been established in some places along the Chinese border.

View image in fullscreen Rameshwor Adhikari at the hospital. Photograph: Sonam Choekyi/The Guardian

Lhakpa Gha’s village, Timure, is one of them. Standing outside a Buddhist monastery on Tuesday afternoon, the 53-year-old says that if she talks, the tears will come.

And as she lists her relatives who were washed away, they do. Her father, brother-in-law, son, daughter-in-law, their four-year-old daughter, her daughter and her sister’s brother. All seven, gone.

Gha and her husband survived because they were in Kathmandu, looking after two of their grandchildren attending school here.

“I lost my whole family,” she says through a translator. “We’ve lost everyone.”

The monastery is housing about 200 people from the upper region who managed to survive – they were higher up on the mountain when the flood hit. Many watched as their loved ones were swept away, their towns flattened.

“The army has not been able to reach the village,” Gha says. “They keep saying our village is high risk but we don’t understand. We are fighting with them. If it’s high risk, you need to act. But they have just said they can’t get in.”

Her son and daughter were doctors in the village – they stayed in Timure so they could keep providing for the family.

“We have nothing,” Gha says. “We depended on my son for money.”

On Monday a UN report into the conditions in the country’s far north said it could take weeks to reach the upper areas – there are hardly any roads left in, and bridges have been washed away.

View image in fullscreen Samdup Tamang and Lhakpa Gha – who lost seven family members – outside a Kathmandu monastery. Photograph: Sonam Choekyi/The Guardian

If the army cannot get in, nor can the aid groups. Amy Sagitta Lefevre from Save the Children says: “Aid is definitely getting through, but to a point.”

Speaking from the agency’s warehouse in Kathmandu, she says its teams have reached Rusawa by road. Aid they can’t get further is stored at the army barracks.

“The challenging bit for rescue workers is the same challenging bit for aid organisations, because we have the same access issues as they do,” she says.

Save the Children is getting kits up the valley that include makeshift tents, so people have somewhere to shelter. It’s also setting up mobile toilets.

“On the ground we’re giving out non-food items,” Lefevre says, “which are blankets, ropes, tarpaulin sheets – because a lot of people are sleeping exposed to the elements, so just sheets in case they need to be protected from the rain.”

Many of the shelters up the valley are overcrowded, so families are being sent farther afield.

View image in fullscreen Amy Sagitta Lefevre at Save the Children’s warehouse in the capital. Photograph: Sonam Choekyi/The Guardian

“We’re also giving out things like buckets, just so people can carry things or wash, if need be.

“And then we have what we call dignity kits … they’re aimed at women, but specifically pregnant women – they have an extra sari, some of the mothers need clothes because they’re still wearing the same clothes they were wearing the day of the disaster.”

About 2,600 children are expected to need medical treatment for “severe wasting” and more than 100 may have been separated from their parents.

Lefevre says it’s impossible to put a timeline on anything. But recognising that the full recovery process could take over a year, Save the Children has set up a field office.

View image in fullscreen Families of missing people wait to register for blood sampling. Photograph: Sonam Choekyi/The Guardian

Its workers are worried about the spread of disease, water contamination, overcrowded shelters and the potential, in the chaos of the recovery, for children to be trafficked.

“This area of Nepal has historically been a hotbed for child trafficking of girls,” she says. “We’ve heard anecdotally that it may have lessened in recent years, but because of this disaster we are now very concerned about the fact that children or girls … could be trafficked.”

सरकार के आग्रह पर मंगलदिन भोर मे लाइन मे लागल दर्जनों मे सं गुरुंग सेहो छथिन्ह. एहि सं पहिने एकटा ऑस्ट्रेलियाई नागरिक पहिल 14 लोक मे सं एक छलाह जे एहि मे शामिल भेलाह. ओ अपन परिवारक संग रहबाक लेल उड़ि गेल छलाह – हुनकर भाइ, नेपाली नागरिक, लापता छथि ।

अधिकारि विदेश मे रिश्तेदार सं कहि रहल छथिन्ह जे हुनकर डीएनए प्रोफाइल ओहि पार भेजल जाए. ऑस्ट्रेलियाई कईटा परिवार क नमूना लेल जा चुकल अछि।

सेना स रामेश्वर अधिकारी कहैत छथि जे हम सब एतय, हुनकर भाई-बहिन स, या सीधा रिश्तेदार स खून क नमूना संग्रह क रहल छी। “घाटी के चारू कात स लोक खून देबय लेल आबि रहल अछि, आ देश भरि के अलग-अलग जगह स।”

डीएनए टेस्टिंग स नेपाल बाढ़ि पीड़ित के खोज मे लागल परिवार के आशा – वीडियो

अधिकारी आगू कहैत छथि: “ई एकटा विपत्ति अछि।एकटा प्राकृतिक विपत्ति।”

पहिल दिन जखन ओ सब सेट केलथि त 37 गोटे के माध्यम स आयल मुदा संख्या बढ़ि रहल अछि – आ सेना लोक के बैसय लेल बेसी छायादार टेंट निकालैत अछि.

अधिकारी चाहैत छथि जे बेसी स बेसी लोक आगू आबय। आब एक हजार सं बेसि लोक के मौत के पुष्टि भ गेल अछि आओर करीब चारि हजार लोक के लापता होय के खबर अछि. बुधदिन भोर धरि एहि मे स 38 गोटे ऑस्ट्रेलियाई छथि।

View image in fullscreen अस्पताल के कर्मचारी खून के नमूना लेबय के तैयारी में. फोटोग्राफ : सोनम चोएकी/द गार्जियन

ई सप्ताह एगो बयान जारी करी क॑ 25 लापता ऑस्ट्रेलियाई के परिवार के सदस्य न॑ “हमरऽ दोस्त आरू प्रियजन क॑ घर वापस लानै लेली” आरू सरकारी सहयोग के आह्वान करलकै ।

सबसँ बेसी प्रभावित इलाका ऊपरी रसुवा जिला के नेपाली परिवार अपन सरकार के बूट आ बचाव उपकरण जमीन पर पहुंचेबा लेल बेसी काज करय लेल अभियान चला रहल अछि।

बाढ़ि के एक सप्ताह भ गेल अछि आओर चीन के सीमा के किछ जगह पर एखन धरि संपर्क नहिं बनल अछि.

फुलस्क्रीन में छवि देखें रामेश्वर अधिकारी अस्पताल में। फोटोग्राफ : सोनम चोएकी/द गार्जियन

ल्हकपा घा’क गाम तिमुरे सेहो ओहि मे सँ एक अछि. मंगलदिन दुपहर मे बौद्ध मठ क बाहर ठाढ़ 53 वर्षीय महिला कहैत छथि जे गप करब त नोर आबि जाएत।

आ जेना-जेना ओ अपन रिश्तेदारक सूची दैत छथि जे बहल छल, ओ सभ सेहो करैत छथि । ओकर पिता, देवर, बेटा, पुतोहु, हुनका लोकनिक चारि सालक बेटी, बेटी आ बहिन’क भाई. सातों, चलि गेलै।

घा आ हुनकर पति एहि लेल बाचि गेलाह जे ओ सब काठमांडू मे छलाह, एतय स्कूल मे पढ़य वाला अपन दू टा पोता-पोती के देखभाल करैत छलाह.

अनुवादक के माध्यम स ओ कहैत छथि जे हम अपन पूरा परिवार कए गंवा देलहुं। “हमरा सभकेँ गमा देल गेल अछि।”

एहि मठ मे ऊपरी क्षेत्र क करीब 200 लोक रहैत छथि जे जीवित रहबा मे सफल रहलाह – जखन बाढ़ि आयल तखन ओ सब पहाड़ पर बेसी ऊँच छलाह। कतेको गोटे देखैत रहलाह जे अपन प्रियजन केँ बहैत गेल, अपन शहर समतल भ' गेल।

घा कहैत छथि, “सेना गाम नहि पहुँचि सकल अछि। “ओ सभ कहैत रहैत छथि जे हमर गाम हाई रिस्क अछि मुदा हमरा सभ केँ नहि बुझल अछि. हम सभ हुनका सभ सँ लड़ि रहल छी. जँ हाई रिस्क अछि त’ अहाँ केँ काज करबाक आवश्यकता अछि. मुदा ओ सभ एखनहि कहने छथि जे ओ सभ भीतर नहि जा सकैत छी.”

हुनकर बेटा-बेटी गाम मे डाक्टर छलाह – ओ सभ तिमुरे मे रहैत छलाह जाहि सँ परिवारक भरण-पोषण करैत रहथि ।

घा कहैत छथि, “हमरा सभ लग किछु नहि अछि। “हम सभ पाइक लेल हमर बेटा पर निर्भर छलहुँ।”

सोमदिन देश केरऽ सुदूर उत्तर केरऽ हालत के बारे म॑ संयुक्त राष्ट्र केरऽ एगो रिपोर्ट म॑ कहलऽ गेलऽ छै कि ऊपरी इलाका म॑ पहुँचै म॑ हफ्ता भर लग॑ सकै छै – शायद ही कोनो सड़क बचलऽ छै, आरू पुल भी बह॑ गेलऽ छै ।

View image in fullscreen समदुप तामांग आ ल्हकपा घा – जे सात परिवार के सदस्य के गंवा देलखिन – काठमांडू मठ के बाहर | फोटोग्राफ : सोनम चोएकी/द गार्जियन

जँ सेना नहि आबि सकैत अछि, आ ने सहायता समूह। सेव द चिल्ड्रेन केरऽ एमी सगिटा लेफेवरे कहै छै: “सहायता निश्चित रूप स॑ गुजरी रहलऽ छै, लेकिन एक हद तलक।”

काठमांडू स्थित एजेंसी के गोदाम सं बजैत ओ कहैत छथि जे ओकर टीम सड़क मार्ग सं रुसावा पहुंच गेल अछि. जे सहायता ओकरा सब केँ आगू नहि भेटि सकैत छैक से सेनाक बैरक मे संग्रहित छैक.

ओ कहैत छथि, “बचाव कर्मीक लेल चुनौतीपूर्ण बिट सहायता संगठन लेल सेहो ओतबे चुनौतीपूर्ण बिट अछि, किया कि हमरा सब लग ओहिना पहुंच क मुद्दा अछि जेना हुनका अछि।”

सेव द चिल्ड्रेन घाटी के ऊपर किट मिल रहल अछि जाहि मे अस्थायी टेंट सेहो शामिल अछि, ताहि लेल लोक के कतहु आश्रय देबय के जगह अछि. मोबाइल शौचालय सेहो लगा रहल अछि.

लेफेवरे कहै छै, “जमीन पर हम गैर-खाद्य वस्तु द॑ रहलऽ छियै, जे कंबल, रस्सी, तिरपाल के चादर छै – कैन्हेंकि बहुत लोग तत्वऽ के सामना करी क॑ सुतलऽ छै, ई लेली बस चादर करी क॑ अगर ओकरा बरसात स॑ बचाबै के जरूरत पड़॑ ।”

घाटी के ऊपर के बहुत रास आश्रय स्थल पर भीड़ बेसी अछि, ताहि लेल परिवार के आओर दूर भेजल जा रहल अछि.

राजधानी में सेव द चिल्ड्रेन के गोदाम में फुलस्क्रीन में छवि देखें एमी सगिट्टा लेफेवरे | फोटोग्राफ : सोनम चोएकी/द गार्जियन

“हम सभ लोटा सन चीज सेहो बाँटि रहल छी, बस एहि लेल जे लोक चीज ल’ जा सकय वा धो सकैत अछि, जरूरत पड़ला पर.

“आ फेर हमरा सभ लग ओ अछि जेकरा हम सभ डिग्निटी किट कहैत छी ... ओ महिला केँ लक्षित अछि, मुदा विशेष रूप सँ गर्भवती महिला केँ – ओकरा सभ लग एकटा अतिरिक्त साड़ी छैक, किछु माय केँ कपड़ा चाही किएक त’ एखनो ओहिना कपड़ा पहिरने छथि जे ओ आपदाक दिन पहिरने छलीह.”

लगभग 2600 बच्चाक कें “गंभीर बर्बादी” कें कारण चिकित्सा कें जरूरत पड़य कें उम्मीद छै आ 100 सं बेसि बच्चाक कें माता-पिता सं अलग भ गेल होयत.

लेफेवरे के कहनाय छनि जे कोनो चीज पर टाइमलाइन लगाबय के काज असंभव अछि. लेकिन ई बात क॑ स्वीकार करी क॑ कि पूरा रिकवरी प्रक्रिया म॑ एक साल स॑ भी अधिक समय लग॑ सकै छै, सेव द चिल्ड्रेन न॑ फील्ड ऑफिस के स्थापना करलकै ।

फुलस्क्रीन मे छवि देखू लापता लोकक परिवार खूनक नमूना लेल पंजीकरण करबाक प्रतीक्षा मे अछि। फोटोग्राफ : सोनम चोएकी/द गार्जियन

एकरऽ मजदूर बीमारी के प्रसार, पानी के प्रदूषण, भीड़भाड़ वाला आश्रय आरू ठीक होय के अराजकता म॑ बच्चा सिनी के तस्करी के संभावना स॑ चिंतित छै ।

ओ कहैत छथि जे नेपालक ई इलाका ऐतिहासिक रूप सँ लड़कीक बाल तस्करीक केंद्र रहल अछि । “हमरा लोकनि किस्सा-कहानी मे सुनने छी जे हालक वर्ष मे ई कम भ’ गेल होयत, मुदा एहि आपदाक कारणेँ आब हमरा सभ केँ एहि बातक बहुत चिंता अछि जे बच्चा वा लड़की ... केर तस्करी भ’ सकैत अछि.”

KATHMANDU, Nepal (AP) — When a wall of water, rocks and mud tore through her remote village in Nepal last week , Pema Tamang and her neighbors fled uphill to a Buddhist shrine that had been rebuilt the previous year after a 2015 earthquake .

The steep mountain folds of the Himalayas, already prone to earthquakes, have seen more frequent flash floods as high mountain glaciers melt , redrawing rivers at sometimes terrifying speed. Residents have had little time to rebuild from one disaster to the next, raising concerns over whether their communities can endure as climate change accelerates.

“We were able to rebuild the stupa only last year after it was destroyed during the earthquake,” Tamang told The Associated Press, referring to the shrine. “Sheltering in it was how we saved our lives from the floods,” she said in a makeshift shelter at a monastery in Kathmandu.

The Aug. 26 floods in Nepal and neighboring China have killed more than 1,000 people and left thousands missing, including hundreds feared trapped in tunnels at hydropower projects. The floods were triggered after a collapse of bedrock and glacier ice sent debris and water surging through multiple Himalayan rivers.

Scientists say it is too early to directly link Wednesday’s catastrophe to global warming. But as Earth’s temperature rises at a faster rate because of the burning of oil, gas and coal, the chances of such disasters increase, especially in the Himalayan mountains, which are warming considerably faster than many other parts of the world.

“Climate change has been playing a large role in the Hindu Kush Himalayas, causing these kinds of complex disasters which have really impacted downstream communities and investments,” said Saswata Sanyal, a disaster risk resilience expert at the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development based in Kathmandu.

Global warming’s effects are heightened in the Himalayas

Sanyal said the region is increasingly confronting hazards that trigger one another.

Warmer temperatures cause high mountain ice to melt, leading to more frequent rockslides, avalanches and floods. An avalanche can dam a river before unleashing a flash flood. Heavy rain after an initial disaster can compound the destruction.

Climate experts say that in some places the danger may become so great that rebuilding is no longer viable, forcing residents to move. Climate change could also have implications for efforts to develop the region through the construction of roads, bridges and hydropower plants.

“The adaptation threshold has been crossed in some areas,” said Manjeet Dhakal, a Nepali climate policy expert and United Nations climate negotiator.

When an earthquake destroys a house, belongings can sometimes be recovered, he said. A catastrophic flood can wipe out not only the house, but the land beneath it, along with roads, water systems, schools and electricity. He said future resettlement would have to incorporate climate risk from the beginning.

The consequences can be mitigated by stricter land-use rules, better assessments before infrastructure is approved, stronger cross-border monitoring and early warning systems.

Sanyal said such warnings need to provide more information on what actions to take. He also suggested prioritizing development in less-dangerous areas, assessing infrastructure for multiple hazards and incorporating the knowledge of Indigenous communities into disaster planning.

Dhakal, the climate negotiator, noted that Nepal has emitted less than 0.1% of the greenhouse gases that cause global warming, even as it grapples with some of its most severe effects.

“We should blame those who are responsible for increasing the global temperature, those who have benefited from the fossil fuel economy for such a long time,” he said. “We can at least use this devastating example as an inspiration to urgently reduce carbon emissions.”

A girl who survived flash flooding at a school converted into a temporary shelter for displaced residents in Bidur, in Nepal's Nuwakot district, Monday, Aug. 31, 2026. [AP Photo/Rajesh Kumar Singh]

As part of the looming humanitarian crisis in the wake of Nepal’s flash flood disaster, the health and safety of tens of thousands of children are at risk in overcrowded shelters without basic necessities. The number at one shelter doubled in a single afternoon, Save the Children said.

The official death toll from the flood disaster in the impoverished South Asian country surged to 1,003 on Tuesday, the sixth day after the disaster, as rescue teams recovered more bodies from eight districts of the country. Sixteen deaths were confirmed on China’s side. The number missing in Nepal has reached 3,916, while China’s state media reported 546 people missing.

Rescue workers are struggling to cope. Hundreds of workers remain trapped in a huge system of mud-filled tunnels at hydropower plants along the Trishuli River. Also among those unaccounted for are several hundred traders, truck drivers and customs-related workers.

Nepal’s road network has collapsed across the central mountainous regions, severely hampering emergency operations. Roads in Rasuwa and Nuwakot have been washed away or buried by landslides, while major routes, including the Trishuli–Mailung–Syabrubesi, Pasang Lhamu and Prithvi highways, are blocked. Entire communities have been isolated, cutting off supplies, rescue equipment and access for emergency teams.

According to a report from the Kathmandu Post on September 1, delays in transporting necessary machinery have forced rescuers to dig by hand at sites like the Upper Trishuli 3A project, through deep mud and debris.

UNICEF reports that about 22,100 children across Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading, Gorkha and Tanahun districts are badly affected. Around 70 percent of children in the worst-hit areas have lost at least one parent. Around 10,500 pregnant and breastfeeding women will require nutritional support, and 2,600 children under five will need treatment for acute malnutrition.

Alice Akunga, UNICEF representative to Nepal, said, “Children across Rasuwa and Dhading saw their lives being literally washed away in front of their eyes in a very short span of time ... With the death toll rising, we know this tragedy is far from over. Children who have survived the floods now face heightened risks of disease, malnutrition, violence and exploitation.” The extensive damage and destruction of health centres mean children and families are not receiving care when they need it most.

At least 18 schools have been destroyed and another 20 damaged. Additionally, according to UNICEF, an estimated 10,000 school-age children now need immediate educational assistance, including access to makeshift learning facilities, substitute educational resources, and psychosocial support. With many routes washed out and villages isolated, large numbers of children remain unable to return to school or reach relief points.

Save the Children reported that one survivor, 57, at a holding center in Nuwakot with his family, said some of his grandchildren were coughing while other children in the center had developed low fevers. He said, “There was a lot of dirt, and we felt like we were going to be sick.” His wife said, “We were out in the open too long, so we have scratchy throats and fever.”

A story about how 900 children were saved has gone viral. Receiving calls about the disaster, principal Rajendra Dawadi of Tribhuvan Trishuli Secondary School in Nuwakot, north-central Nepal, quickly decided to evacuate, telling the children to flee to higher ground. Moments later, a torrent of mud, boulders, and water engulfed the school, flattening classrooms and washing away entire structures.

In another story, Karbir Gaire, a customs and information officer at Nepal’s Rasuwa Customs Office, saw the massive flood coming and saved himself and several others by instantly running uphill. Later, the muddy flood washed away the surrounding structures. According to Gaire, even seconds were decisive: Only those who saw the disaster coming and fled for their lives were saved, while others perished.

This indicates how many more could have been saved if a robust early warning system (EWS) were functioning in Nepal. The EWS in flood-hit northern districts faced an unprecedented failure. Nepal’s flood gauges are intended to warn about dangers from monsoon rains, but the system was not built to warn about flash floods. Upstream monitoring stations in Nepal were swept away by the flooding before alerts could be sent.

Austin Lord, an anthropologist, told the New York Times on August 27 that the landslide was in a “blind spot” on the northern side of Nepal’s Langtang mountain range, an area that he said was scarcely populated and barely monitored by geologists.

The inadequacy of the warning system was not the only failure. The floods inflicted tremendous devastation on riverbank villages, hydropower projects, and the highway network. The Kathmandu Post noted in one of its columns on August 27 that the riverside infrastructure is designed based on 50-to-100-year historical averages that are badly outdated because “climate change has altered weather patterns, introducing cloudbursts, intense debris flows, and heavy sediment loads.”

This is not simply a natural disaster but one created by man-made global warming of the Hindu Kush Himalaya. It is known as the “Third Pole” because it holds the largest ice reserves outside the Arctic and Antarctic regions. The melting of glaciers, the formation of unstable moraine-dammed lakes, and the increasing frequency of Glacial Lake Outburst Floods (GLOFs) are the physical processes. The social processes—decades of under-investment in infrastructure, the commodification of land and water, and the prioritization of private profit over public safety under capitalism—are what turned those processes into a human disaster.

Despite the region’s volatility, successive Nepali governments have failed to build resilient infrastructure, to relocate vulnerable communities on a humane basis, or to build effective early-warning systems and evacuation corridors that could have saved lives. Responsibility also rests with the major imperialist powers that have kept Nepal economically backward and impoverished and used their pittance in aid to further their own economic and strategic interests.

मध्य पहाड़ी क्षेत्र मे नेपालक सडक जाल ढहला सँ आपातकालीन परिचालन मे भारी बाधा पहुँचल अछि । रसुवा आरू नुवाकोट केरऽ सड़क भूस्खलन स॑ बह॑ गेलऽ छै या दबी गेलऽ छै, जबकि त्रिशुली–मैलुंग–स्याब्रुबेसी, पासंग ल्हामू आरू पृथ्वी राजमार्ग सहित प्रमुख मार्ग अवरुद्ध छै । पूरा समुदाय क॑ अलग-थलग करी देलऽ गेलऽ छै, जेकरा स॑ आपूर्ति, बचाव उपकरण आरू आपातकालीन टीम लेली पहुँच बंद होय गेलऽ छै ।

काठमांडू पोस्टके १ सितम्बरके रिपोर्टके अनुसार आवश्यक मशीनरीके परिवहनमे देरीके कारण उद्धारक अपर त्रिशूली ३ ए परियोजना सन स्थलमे, गहरे थाल आ मलबाके माध्यमसँ हाथसँ खोदब बाध्य भेल अछि ।

यूनिसेफ के रिपोर्ट के अनुसार पूरा रसुवा, नुवाकोट, धडिंग, गोरखा आरू तनाहुन जिला के लगभग 22,100 बच्चा बहुत प्रभावित छै । सब सं बेसि प्रभावित इलाकाक मे लगभग 70 प्रतिशत बच्चाक कें कम सं कम एकटा माता-पिता कें मौत भ गेल छै. लगभग 10,500 गर्भवती आ स्तनपान करा रहल महिलाआक कें पोषण संबंधी सहायता कें आवश्यकता होयत, आ पांच साल सं कम उम्र कें 2,600 बच्चाक कें तीव्र कुपोषण कें इलाज कें आवश्यकता होयत.

नेपाल मे यूनिसेफ के प्रतिनिधि ऐलिस अकुंगा कहलनि जे, “रसुवा आ धडिंग भरिक बच्चा सब बहुत कम समय मे अपन जीवन के अक्षरशः आँखि के सामने बहैत देखलक... मृत्यु के संख्या बढ़ला के संग हमरा सब के पता अछि जे ई त्रासदी खत्म होयब बहुत दूर अछि।बाढ़ि स बचल बच्चा सब के आब बीमारी, कुपोषण, हिंसा आ शोषण के बढ़ल खतरा के सामना करय पड़ैत अछि।” स्वास्थ्य केंद्रक कें व्यापक नुकसान आ तबाही कें मतलब छै की बच्चाक आ परिवारक कें देखभाल नहि भ रहल छै जखन ओकरा बेसि जरूरत छै.

कम स कम 18टा स्कूल नष्ट भ गेल अछि आओर 20टा आओर क्षतिग्रस्त भ गेल अछि। एकर अलावा, यूनिसेफ कें अनुसार, अनुमानित 10,000 स्कूली उम्र कें बच्चाक कें आब तत्काल शैक्षिक सहायता कें जरूरत छै, जइ मे अस्थायी सीखय कें सुविधाक कें पहुंच, वैकल्पिक शैक्षिक संसाधनक, आ मनोसामाजिक सहायता शामिल छै. बहुत रास मार्ग बहल आ गाम अलग-थलग भ गेल अछि, एहि लेल पैघ संख्या मे बच्चा स्कूल वापस नहि आबि सकैत अछि या राहत बिंदु पर पहुंचबा मे असमर्थ अछि।

सेव द चिल्ड्रेन केरऽ रिपोर्ट छै कि अपनऽ परिवार के साथ नुवाकोट केरऽ एगो होल्डिंग सेंटर म॑ 57 साल केरऽ एगो बची गेलऽ व्यक्ति न॑ कहलकै कि ओकरऽ कुछ पोता-पोती खांसी करी रहलऽ छै जबकि सेंटर केरऽ कुछ बच्चा सिनी क॑ कम बोखार होय गेलऽ छै । ओ कहलनि, “बहुत गंदगी छल, आ हमरा सभ केँ लागल जेना बीमार पड़ब।” पत्नी बजलीह, “हम सभ बेसी काल खुला मे बाहर छलहुँ, तेँ हमरा सभक कंठ खरोंचैत अछि आ बोखार सेहो अछि।”

900 बच्चा के कोना बचाओल गेल, एहि पर एकटा कहानी वायरल भ गेल अछि. आपदा के बारे में फोन आबै के बाद उत्तर-मध्य नेपाल के नुवाकोट स्थित त्रिभुवन त्रिशूली माध्यमिक विद्यालय के प्राचार्य राजेन्द्र दावाडी जल्दी-जल्दी बाहर निकलै के फैसला करलकै, बच्चा सब के ऊंच जगह प भागै लेली कहलकै । किछुए क्षणक बाद थाल-कादो, बोल्डर आ पानिक धार स्कूल के घेरि लेलक, जाहि सं कक्षा समतल भ गेल आ पूरा संरचना बह गेल.

एकटा आओर कथा मे नेपाल के रसुवा सीमा शुल्क कार्यालय के सीमा शुल्क आओर सूचना अधिकारी कर्बीर गैरे भारी बाढ़ि आबि रहल देखि तुरंत चढ़ाई पर दौड़ि क’ अपना आओर कतेको लोक के बचा लेलखिन्ह. बाद मे थाल-कादोक बाढ़ि आसपासक संरचना सभ केँ बहौलक। गैरे के अनुसार सेकेंड भी निर्णायक छेलै: केवल वू लोगऽ के उद्धार होय गेलै जे आपदा के आबै वाला देखलकै आरू अपनऽ जान बचाबै लेली भागी गेलै, जबकि कुछ लोगऽ के नाश होय गेलै।
